Science.title: A humpback whale was spotted in a California river, 60 miles from its Pacific Ocean home
Science.summary: Denny Glover was hoping for a big catch when he went fishing with buddies on the Sacramento River, but he wasn't expecting a fully grown humpback whale.

Science.title: Bringing ice sheets to life: Releasing a dynamic ice sheet modeling workflow for Australia's climate model
Science.summary: Ice sheets are fundamental components of the Earth system. Antarctica and Greenland, the two ice sheets currently on Earth, don't just affect their own regions: What happens on these vast masses of land ice influences weather, climate, society and the environment around the planet.

Science.title: Reconstructing the Great Miami Hurricane of 1926
Science.summary: The first storm warning for the Miami area wasn't issued until only a few hours before the powerful cyclone made landfall just south of downtown, leaving residents with little time to prepare for what would become the hurricane of their nightmares.

Science.title: A molecular bridge connects two signaling pathways critical for pollen development
Science.summary: Cells rely on complex signaling networks in which different molecular pathways communicate with one another. Small GTPases act as molecular switches in these networks, controlling diverse cellular processes such as intracellular transport and cell morphogenesis. Although crosstalk between different families of small GTPases is established in animal cells, whether and how such crosstalk occurs in plants has remained largely unknown.

Science.title: Australia's vast Nullarbor Plain hides deep caves that can teach us about alien worlds
Science.summary: Stretching more than 200,000 square kilometers (77,000 square miles) across southern Australia, the vast, flat plains of the Nullarbor mark one of the world's largest regions of limestone. It formed when an ancient shallow sea retreated some 14 million years ago.

Science.title: Loss of Y chromosome in men could be an early warning sign of cancer
Science.summary: A study initiated by Dr. Dan Theodorescu, a physician-scientist at the University of Arizona Cancer Center, revealed that the loss of the Y chromosome in men's body tissue could pave the way for cancer to develop. According to research recently published in JCI Insights, the loss of the chromosome, which is common in men as they age, creates a preneoplastic field effect, a hidden zone of genetic vulnerability in normal tissue that provides fertile ground for cancer to develop.

Science.title: Global population dataset uses buildings to reveal people's daily movement patterns
Science.summary: Researchers at the Department of Energy's (DOE) Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) have released LandScan Mosaic, a next-generation global population distribution dataset that estimates where people are by modeling how buildings are used and occupied throughout the day. Built on the foundation of ORNL's widely used LandScan Global, one of the world's most accurate population distribution datasets, Mosaic's enhancements will improve disaster response, humanitarian assistance, infrastructure planning and national security missions worldwide.

Science.title: Sea surface temperature biases shift the North Pacific jet stream southward, study finds
Science.summary: Climate models are numerical models used to project future climate change. They simulate the climate from the present into the future by calculating changes in the atmosphere, ocean and other components of the climate system. However, simulations of the present-day climate do not perfectly reproduce observations and contain various biases. The model characteristics that cause these biases can also affect simulations of the future climate. Understanding the causes and impacts of present-day climate biases is therefore important for improving the reliability of future climate projections.

Science.title: Two-color light steers electrons through graphene's transient topological state
Science.summary: The electronic properties of materials are typically determined by their structure under normal, undisturbed conditions, when they are in a state known as equilibrium. Intense light beams, however, can temporarily reshape a material's electronic band structure (i.e., the range of energy states available to electrons), potentially giving rise to new electronic behaviors.

Science.summary: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 September 19 –… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Night SkyAnnotation A […]

Science.title: Scientists hope deeper-rooted soybeans can withstand climate extremes and store more carbon
Science.summary: Research scientist Ashish Rajurkar kneels in the dirt, lifting a large clod of soil tangled around a soybean plant. He knocks away pieces of earth from the plant's roots, which slope straight down instead of out to the side like typical soybean plants.

Science.title: Scientists simulate cosmic crashes to test whether icy moons gain or lose their ability to sustain life
Science.summary: Many of the moons orbiting Saturn, Uranus and Neptune likely conceal oceans of liquid water beneath miles of icy shell. Because life as we know it needs water, these buried oceans rank among the most promising places to search for life beyond Earth.

Science.title: Medieval Chinese skeleton may reveal first evidence of a brutal punishment
Science.summary: Ancient Chinese authorities used many creative ways to punish people, often with methods designed to mark them for life. One brutal example mentioned repeatedly in historical texts is cutting off a person's nose. However, archaeologists in China have never found skeletal evidence to prove that it occurred. But that may have changed following the discovery of a skeleton of a woman who lived in China about 700 years ago.

Science.title: To read 2,000-year-old burned scrolls, scientists burn their own
Science.summary: Douglas Seiler painstakingly sourced papyrus and reed pens from Egypt and traditional lampblack ink from Japan, then paid some high school students to inscribe the papyrus with lines from Star Wars and the Bible and a quote from the '60s sci-fi TV show The Outer Limits.

Science.title: Protein map reveals how red blood cells rapidly adjust to low oxygen
Science.summary: Scientists map the hidden protein network that helps red blood cells adapt to oxygen

Science.title: Scientists build a DNA computer that can perform calculations in a drop of water
Science.summary: This programmable DNA computer can perform arithmetic without the continuous energy input needed by other systems.

Science.title: Meet Earth's newest wild cat species, the first named in over a century
Science.summary: A previously unknown cat species has been identified in plain sight: at a wildlife sanctuary in Bolivia, where the small, spotted feline had been living for years.

Science.title: Power breeds suspicion: In cases of wrongdoing, people point to leaders more quickly
Science.summary: People with power are more quickly singled out as the culprit when something goes wrong but it is unclear who made the mistake. That is shown by a series of studies by researchers at the University of Amsterdam. In one, they analyzed almost 100,000 everyday conflicts on the Reddit page "Am I the Asshole?" According to the researchers, people with power are more readily blamed because others think they can "get away with anything." The findings are published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology.

Science.title: How the malaria parasite boosts its transmission potential under stress conditions
Science.summary: The malaria parasite is able to detect changes in its host's environment and respond by increasing the production of sexual forms capable of being transmitted to mosquitoes. A study led by the Barcelona Institute for Global Health (ISGlobal) identifies the molecular mechanism underlying this process. The findings, published in Nature Microbiology, answer what has been one of the major unanswered questions in malaria research for decades.

Science.title: North Korea's nuclear testing may have triggered hundreds of earthquakes over several years
Science.summary: Between 2006 and 2017, North Korea conducted six underground nuclear tests at its vast testing site at Mount Mantap in North Hamgyong province. Typically, underground explosions trigger an intense burst of minor earthquakes that die down once testing stops. But geologists have detected far more seismic activity after the final detonation, and it has persisted for years.

Science.title: The monsters that weren't: Dinosaur and tusked-beast claims in San rock art unravel
Science.summary: For decades, an idea has grown in paleontology that, long before scientists began digging up and reconstructing dinosaur bones, the Indigenous San and Basotho in southern Africa noticed them too, incorporating them into songs, myths and immortalizing them on cave walls. But under closer scrutiny, these claims begin to crumble.

Science.title: How narwhal 'scientists' track Arctic warming
Science.summary: The fight against climate change has a new, spiral-tusked ally: the narwhal.

Science.title: Improving urban flood forecasting with real-time hazardous rainfall detection
Science.summary: The Korea Institute of Civil Engineering and Building Technology (KICT) announced that it will apply its early detection technology for quasi-stationary linear rainbands and sudden localized torrential rainfall to the Urban Flood Forecasting Platform operated by the Han River Flood Control Office in Korea for urban flood forecasting.

Science.title: Peer sexual harassment emerges early, highlighting need for prevention before Grade 4
Science.summary: Sexual harassment between peers begins as early as Grade 4 and continues throughout lower secondary school. Most of those who sexually harass others have also experienced harassment themselves. These are among the findings of a doctoral thesis in psychology by Aziz-Kaan Dönmez from the University of Gothenburg, who studied peer sexual harassment among Swedish children and adolescents in Grades 4–9. Dönmez will defend his thesis on October 2.

Science.title: An 'impossible' black hole merger may finally be solved thanks to Einstein's relativity — but it raises an even bigger mystery
Science.summary: New research suggests that a perplexing signal created by a pair of colliding black holes may have been warped by a space-time phenomenon known as gravitational lensing. This theory could finally explain the "impossible" size of the merging singularities, but it also poses a new problem.

Science.title: Why does blond hair tend to darken with age?
Science.summary: Some children have blond hair that darkens as they grow up. What causes this change?

Science.title: Kids involved with child protective services miss much more school than their peers
Science.summary: Across the country, kids are settling into new school-year routines. Parents buy backpacks, teachers arrange desks and lesson plans, and friends reconnect. But in recent years, empty chairs are becoming a more common sight—especially in classrooms where students are already facing the most adversity.

Science.title: Europe can lower emissions without deindustrializing, say researchers
Science.summary: The European Union has committed to achieving climate neutrality by 2050, a process that will require rapid and substantial reductions in greenhouse gas emissions across all economic sectors.

Science.title: At an old steel site in Pittsburgh, bacteria evolved to survive—and eat—industrial pollution
Science.summary: Across Appalachia and the Rust Belt region, including throughout the city of Pittsburgh, former industrial sites are being transformed into new neighborhoods, research centers and technology hubs.

Science.title: NASA Invites Media to Albania Artemis Accords Signing Ceremony
Science.summary: The Republic of Albania will sign the Artemis Accords during a ceremony at 12 p.m. EDT on Monday, Sept. 21, at NASA Headquarters in Washington, becoming the 73rd country signatory. NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson will host Albania’s Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs Ferit Hoxha and Ambassador of the Republic of Albania to the […]

Science.title: Florida scrub-jays attempt to breed at unusually young age after large-scale translocation
Science.summary: For nearly two decades, biologist Lauren Deaner has worked with Florida scrub-jays, contributing to population recovery efforts and translocations. Now, as a doctoral researcher in UCF's integrative biology program, she is using that field experience to investigate how genetics, behavior and population dynamics influence the long-term recovery of imperiled species.

Science.title: How rural policing gaps can make escaping domestic violence harder
Science.summary: Before murdering Molly Ticehurst in April 2024, court documents show Daniel Billings had threatened to exploit the limits of policing in her country town: "I will come in the middle of the night … The police won't stop me. I will get to you quicker than they will."

Science.title: Workplace AI adoption remains slow, informal and uneven, survey finds
Science.summary: Despite the rapid development of generative AI and the high level of public interest, the use of AI in the day-to-day work of many employees is not yet the norm. This is the finding of the third wave of the Konstanz AI study, for which a total of 1,105 employees were surveyed in May 2026. The proportion of employees who use AI in their work rose only slightly from 35% to 38% compared with the previous year.

Science.title: Rethinking how we assess students could improve their well-being
Science.summary: When you were in school, what stressed you out the most? For many students, classroom assessments—graded tests, quizzes, group work, presentations, labs and the like—would be near the top of the list.
